implementation_notes: The idiomatic Java answer is an explicit copy constructor or static copy factory: it returns a fully constructed, correctly typed object, works with final fields, keeps one construction path (validation plus defensive copies) and can be chained by subclasses that need to copy their own fields - Effective Java item 13 prefers it over Cloneable. Nested mutable state gets copied field by field in that same place, so the decision to share or to copy is visible in the code.
pitfalls: A copy constructor that assigns a mutable field directly (this.list = other.list) shares it; copy collections and arrays explicitly.
final fields cannot be fixed up after cloning, which is why the copy constructor must build the object completely in one pass.
Subclasses must call super(other) or inherited fields are not copied - and a copy constructor cannot be virtual, so polymorphic copying still needs an overridable copy() method.

variants.name: Cloneable + super.clone() (+ deep copy of mutable fields)
variants.implementation_notes: The JDK mechanism: implement Cloneable, override the protected clone() with a public covariant return, call super.clone() for the field-for-field copy and then deep-copy the mutable fields. It is the only way to clone an object whose concrete type you do not know when the hierarchy already implements it, and the runtime guarantees x.clone().getClass() == x.getClass() as long as every class chains super.clone(). Otherwise prefer the copy constructor: the contract is only a shallow copy and it forces CloneNotSupportedException bookkeeping.
pitfalls: Forgetting the deep-copy step leaves arrays and collections shared between original and clone - the classic shallow-clone bug.
clone() must call super.clone(); a clone built with new returns the wrong runtime class for subclasses and breaks the convention.
Object.clone() skips constructors, so validation, defensive copies and registration performed there are not applied to the clone.
